content: Adolescent girls and young women are at a significantly higher risk of acquiring HIV compared to their male counterparts, as well as older women and men. Between 2016 and 2022, the Central African Network for HIV/AIDS Ethics and Law (RCED), in collaboration with the Ministry of Justice, the Ministry of Health, and UNAIDS, worked to revise the 2006 law that mandated parental consent for HIV testing in adolescents under the age of 18. A critical component of the revised law was the reduction of the age of consent for HIV testing, which was informed by updated scientific evidence and the specific context of Central Africa. Efforts to amend the age-of-consent law included hosting stakeholder consultations to draft the law, forming an expert group to validate and revise the draft, presenting the rationale for the new law to parliamentarians, and securing its adoption by the National Assembly in November 2022, followed by the President's signature in December 2022. The enacted law now permits adolescents as young as 12 years old to consent to HIV testing, prioritizing the health and well-being of the child over certain social considerations. This law also strengthens the rights of individuals living with HIV and those at high risk of infection, aligning with the latest scientific advancements in HIV prevention, testing, and treatment. The revised law mandates free and informed consent before screening, ensures the confidentiality of test results, and prohibits all forms of stigma and discrimination against people living with HIV. Key factors contributing to the success of this policy reform included adequate resources, dedicated staff to oversee the process, and active engagement with parliamentarians to garner support for the law. This initiative was led by the Ministry of Health and UNAIDS in the Central African Republic in 2022. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that all pregnant women undergo testing for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) at least once, ideally during their first antenatal care visit. Dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are suggested as the initial test in antenatal care settings and for maternal retesting where feasible. However, dual RDTs should not be used for pregnant individuals already on antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV or those previously diagnosed and treated for syphilis during the current pregnancy. In such cases, separate tests should be conducted based on national algorithms. Pregnant women who test negative for HBsAg may be offered hepatitis B vaccination without further serological testing if unavailable. Follow-up for all newborns includes timely hepatitis B vaccination at birth and subsequent doses to ensure infants born to mothers with chronic HBV infection receive the recommended three doses of the vaccine, especially if the birth dose was missed. Services for pregnant and postpartum women should be as integrated as possible, with HIV testing serving as an entry point for broader pregnancy care and prevention services, including screening and treatment for other infections (e.g., STIs, viral hepatitis, and TB), HIV prevention, and sexual and reproductive health services. Pregnant and breastfeeding women diagnosed with HIV should initiate ART immediately or as soon as possible after diagnosis, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 cell count, and continue treatment for life. Pregnant HIV-negative women at substantial risk of acquiring HIV should be offered pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) during pregnancy and breastfeeding, with regular testing or self-testing as per national guidelines. Counseling should emphasize the benefits of PrEP during this period. Network-based testing is recommended for pregnant women and their partners, including social network testing and partner services, with mutual disclosure support in all settings. Self-tests for HIV and syphilis may also be considered, particularly for pregnant women to distribute to their male partners. Retesting HIV-negative pregnant women is optimally done during the third trimester, with additional postpartum retesting for breastfeeding mothers in high HIV-burden areas or among key populations. In Ghana, the introduction of dual HIV/syphilis testing in antenatal care (ANC) settings significantly increased syphilis testing coverage from 53% in 2018 to 91% in 2021. This initiative, led by the Ghana Health Service and the National AIDS/STI Programme, involved extensive stakeholder engagement, verification studies to select appropriate tests, and training of service providers. The dual tests were found to be convenient and cost-effective, reducing procurement costs by at least 16%. Despite challenges such as incomplete training and suboptimal partner treatment, the adoption of dual testing has been instrumental in improving syphilis testing coverage and advancing Ghana's triple elimination strategy. For infants and children, early diagnosis and treatment of HIV are critical, as untreated HIV-infected infants face a mortality rate of approximately 35–40% within the first year of life. Early infant diagnosis (EID) and same-day point-of-care testing significantly improve survival rates and clinical outcomes, reducing the HIV reservoir in the population. WHO recommends nucleic acid testing (NAT) at birth or within two days, complemented by additional testing at 4–6 weeks of age or the earliest opportunity thereafter. Infants with an initial positive virological test result should start ART immediately, even as confirmatory testing is conducted. Testing strategies for infants and children include facility-based testing, community outreach, and network-based approaches. HIV-exposed infants and children should be tested whenever they present with illness, attend outpatient or immunization clinics, or are admitted to malnutrition or TB wards. Family and household testing for children living with HIV-positive parents or siblings is also recommended. For children and adolescents who have experienced sexual abuse, WHO advises offering HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), emergency contraception, and presumptive treatment for STIs where laboratory testing is not feasible. Additionally, HPV vaccination should be offered to adolescent girls aged 9–14 years as per national guidelines. To eliminate pediatric HIV/AIDS by 2030, scaling up access to testing and treatment for infants and children is a global health priority. Comprehensive testing approaches, including same-day testing, confirmatory testing, and end-of-exposure diagnosis, are essential to ensure timely initiation of ART and improved health outcomes.
